history.title: Design a Government That Cannot Be Trusted

data.body:
**Due:** (your teacher will tell you)

The framers had a strange design problem: build a government strong enough to work, but assume the people running it will eventually be selfish, ambitious, or wrong. Everything in the Constitution follows from that assumption.

1. Read **Rules for the Rule-Makers** — look for the phrase "what if the wrong person wins?"
2. Learn the terms in the **Glossary**, then win the **Crossword** and the **Matching** game.
3. Use the **Three Branches** chart as your map while you work.
4. Walk the **Road to Ratification** timeline — the arguments are still being had today.
5. Sort the powers in **Who Can Do That?**
6. Take the quiz — it asks you to reason like a framer, not recite.
7. Take a position in the **Sentence Frames**. Disagreeing with the framers is allowed if you can argue it.
8. Lock the ideas in with **Remember the Machine** — study the example aid, then make one your own.
9. Finish with **Proposal: Rules for Our Own Rule-Makers** — use what you learned on a real problem, and mark every guess as a guess.

Big question to hold the whole time: is a slow government a broken one, or a safe one? ⚖️

history.title: Rules for the Rule-Makers
history.data:
## Rules for the Rule-Makers

In the summer of 1787, fifty-five men locked themselves in a hot Philadelphia room with the windows kept shut so nobody could overhear. They had been sent to patch up the failing Articles of Confederation. Instead they threw them out and started over.

Their problem was not how to build a government. Their problem was how to build one that would still be safe when the wrong people were running it.

The Articles had produced a government too weak to function: no general power to tax directly, no separate national executive, and only limited national courts and enforcement tools. But the framers had just fought a war against a king, and a strong government sounded like the thing they had escaped. So they invented a machine designed to work while distrusting its own operators.

First they split power three ways. The **legislative** branch — Congress — writes laws. The **executive** branch, headed by the President, carries them out. The **judicial** branch, the courts, decides what they mean. This is **separation of powers**. Its logic is simple: no single person or group ever holds the whole thing.

Then they went further and gave each branch weapons against the others — **checks and balances**. Congress passes a bill; the President can veto it; Congress can override that veto with a two-thirds vote in each chamber. The President appoints judges; the Senate must confirm them. Courts can strike down laws as unconstitutional. The House can impeach a President or a judge; the Senate can remove the official after a trial and the required two-thirds vote to convict.

They also split power a second way, between the national government and the states — **federalism** — so that even a captured national government does not control everything.

All of this makes government slow. That is not a bug. James Madison argued in Federalist No. 51 that "ambition must be made to counteract ambition" — that the safest system is one where powerful people are constantly blocked by other powerful people who want something different.

It is worth naming honestly what this document did not do. Its three-fifths **compromise** used three-fifths of the enslaved population when calculating state representation in the House and shares of direct taxes. That population formula increased slaveholding states' political power compared with not counting enslaved people; it did not give enslaved people the vote or end slavery. The fraction described a political calculation, never a person's humanity or worth. Voting rules varied by state and excluded many people. Most women could not vote, but some property-qualified unmarried women and free Black residents could vote in New Jersey until its law narrowed eligibility in 1807. The system left major exclusions and protections for slavery in place. Later amendments, organizing, laws and enforcement expanded rights, through a struggle that did not end with changing the text.

That is the real inheritance: not a perfect document, but a repairable one, plus the argument about how to repair it. That argument is still running, and you are now in it.

data.title: Remember the Machine
data.instructions: Each card locks in facts from Rules for the Rule-Makers. Study the example aid, make it yours, and explain how it leads back to the design of the government.
data.sourceExcerpt: The legislative branch writes laws. The executive branch carries them out. The judicial branch decides what they mean. Congress passes a bill; the President can veto it; Congress can override with two-thirds. The President appoints judges; the Senate must confirm them. Courts can strike down laws. The amendment process is how later generations forced it open.

essentialFacts: Legislative (Congress: House and Senate) writes laws and controls spending.
Executive (the President and agencies) carries out laws and commands the military.
Judicial (the Supreme Court and lower courts) interprets laws and can rule them unconstitutional.
cards.aiExample: L-E-J: Lawmakers Enforce? No — Lawmakers write, Executives Enforce, Judges Judge. 'Legislate, Execute, Judge' — the three verbs are the three branches.
cards.mapping: Each branch name is already a verb in disguise: legislate, execute, judge. Saying the verbs keeps the jobs from swapping.
scaffoldSteps: Turn each branch name into its verb.
Attach the main body: Congress, President, courts.
Say one power each has over another.
coachPrompts: Does your aid show that the judicial branch decides meaning, not just punishment?
cards.reasoningPrompt: How does each verb in your aid match a branch's job?

cards.mapping: The different locks represent distinct checks with different procedures and thresholds. The analogy reminds us to ask who acts and under what rule; it does not mean every decision has an immediate opposite move.

Find the counter-move to each power.
Pick a game or sport where every move has an answer and map the branches onto it.

cards.target: The road to ratification and the amendment door
essentialFacts: 1781: Articles of Confederation in force, with no general direct taxing power, no separate national executive and only limited national courts. 1787: Constitution written in Philadelphia.
1788: New Hampshire becomes the ninth state to ratify, meeting Article VII's threshold among ratifying states. The new federal government begins operations in 1789.
1791 Bill of Rights: ten amendments added because Anti-Federalists demanded explicit protections.

The proposal route used for all 27 amendments is a two-thirds vote in each chamber of Congress. Article V also permits a convention called on application of two-thirds of state legislatures. Ratification requires three-fourths of states, through legislatures or conventions as Congress specifies.
cards.aiExample: Articles fail (1781) → Philadelphia writes (1787) → ninth state ratifies (1788) → Bill of Rights repairs (1791) → the door stays open (27 amendments). Weak, Write, Ratify, Repair, Repeat.
cards.mapping: Five beats in order, and the last one is the point of the reading: the document is repairable, and the sequence shows the first repair happening within four years.
scaffoldSteps: Put the four dates in order with one word each.
Add a fifth beat for what the amendment process makes possible.
Name one later repair (13th, 15th, or 19th Amendment).
coachPrompts: Where in your sequence do the Anti-Federalists win something?
cards.reasoningPrompt: How does your sequence show that the Constitution was built to be repaired?

history.title: Think Like a Framer

questions.question: Why did the framers deliberately design a government that acts slowly?
options: Because communication in the 1780s was slow anyway, so speed was impossible
So that no single group could seize control quickly or act unchecked
To give states enough time to ignore federal laws they disagreed with
Because they expected the country to stay small and rural for a long time
questions.correctAnswer: So that no single group could seize control quickly or act unchecked

questions.question: Congress passes a bill and the President vetoes it. What can Congress do next?
options: Ask the Supreme Court to sign the bill instead
Nothing — a veto is final
Override the veto with a two-thirds vote in both chambers
Send it to the states for ratification
questions.correctAnswer: Override the veto with a two-thirds vote in both chambers

questions.question: What was the main weakness of the Articles of Confederation?
options: It gave the President too much military power over the individual states
It created too many federal courts, which argued with each other
It required every state to hold its elections on exactly the same day
The national government could not tax or enforce its own laws
questions.correctAnswer: The national government could not tax or enforce its own laws

questions.question: The Great Compromise settled a fight between large and small states. What did it create?
options: A House based on population and a Senate with equal seats per state
A single chamber where every state had one vote
A council of governors that could veto Congress
A rule that the President must come from a small state
questions.correctAnswer: A House based on population and a Senate with equal seats per state

questions.question: Which statement about the original Constitution is accurate?
options: It guaranteed voting rights to all adult citizens regardless of race, sex, or property
It immediately outlawed slavery in every state as soon as it was ratified
It used three-fifths of the enslaved population in representation and direct-tax calculations without giving enslaved people the vote
It gave women the same political rights as men, including the right to vote
questions.correctAnswer: It used three-fifths of the enslaved population in representation and direct-tax calculations without giving enslaved people the vote

questions.question: Madison wrote that 'ambition must be made to counteract ambition.' Explain what he meant and give one example from the Constitution.
questions.expectedAnswer: He meant the system should use officials' self-interest against each other rather than relying on them to be good. Example: the President wants power but Congress can override vetoes and impeach, and courts can strike down laws — each branch's ambition blocks the others.

questions.question: The reading calls the Constitution 'not a perfect document, but a repairable one.' Explain what makes it repairable and name one repair later generations made.
questions.expectedAnswer: Article V provides ways to amend the text. Examples include the Thirteenth Amendment prohibiting slavery and involuntary servitude except as punishment for crime, the Fifteenth prohibiting denial of voting rights on account of race, color or previous condition of servitude, and the Nineteenth prohibiting denial on account of sex. Accept a correct relevant example; amendments required further organizing, laws and enforcement to secure access.

reflections.text: Is a slow government a broken one or a safe one? Take a side and give your strongest reason.
If you could add one amendment today, what would it say — and which branch would it limit?

data.question: Why did they nail the windows shut in Philadelphia? 🪟
data.answer: Secrecy. They wanted delegates to argue and change their minds freely without newspapers reporting every shift. It also made the room brutally hot all summer, which some historians think hurried the work along.

data.question: Has the Constitution ever been rewritten?
data.answer: Never rewritten — only amended, 27 times so far. Ten of those came at once as the Bill of Rights in 1791. Thousands of amendments have been proposed and rejected.

data.question: Why is amending it so hard?
data.answer: Article V offers more than one route. Every amendment so far was proposed by a two-thirds vote in each chamber of Congress; a convention can also be called on application of two-thirds of state legislatures. Ratification needs three-fourths of states, through legislatures or conventions as Congress chooses. These high thresholds make change possible but demanding.

data.question: Who decides what the Constitution 'means'? ⚖️
data.answer: The courts, ultimately the Supreme Court — a power called judicial review that the document does not explicitly grant. The Court claimed it in Marbury v. Madison in 1803, and it stuck.

data.question: Did everyone in 1787 like this plan?
data.answer: Definitely not. Anti-Federalists warned it created a national government too strong and lacking explicit protections for individuals. They lost the ratification fight but won the Bill of Rights, which exists because of their pressure.

data.question: Is the Constitution the oldest one in the world?
data.answer: It is the oldest written national constitution still in force, which is a real distinction — though several countries have older uncodified constitutional traditions.

data.title: Rules for Our Own Rule-Makers
data.instructions: Draft a short constitution for a student council, designed the way the framers designed theirs: assume the people in charge will sometimes be selfish or wrong, and build in checks that keep working anyway.
data.fitReason: The lesson's big idea is designing for distrust of your own operators. Writing rules for a real student body forces students to use separation of powers and checks instead of reciting them.

brief.context: Your school is starting a student council that will control a small activities budget, plan events, and hear complaints about school rules. The principal has asked students to propose how it should be organized so that no single person or group can run it for their friends.
brief.audience: The principal and the students who will vote on the proposal
brief.drivingQuestion: How should the student council divide its powers and check itself so that it still works fairly when the wrong people win an election?
brief.seedDirection: Start with the framers' question: what happens if the wrong person wins? Then give every power a counter-power.
lockedLessonFacts: Separation of powers: legislative writes laws, executive carries them out, judicial decides what they mean; no one group holds the whole thing.
Checks and balances: veto and override, appointment and confirmation, judicial review, impeachment.
The framers designed a slow government on purpose so no single group could seize control quickly.
The Articles lacked a general direct taxing power and a separate national executive, and had limited enforcement tools and courts. These limits helped drive the 1787 convention.

The original Constitution left major exclusions and protections for slavery. Later amendments, organizing, laws and enforcement expanded rights; changing the text alone did not instantly secure equal access.
openQuestions: Who decides when a council member has broken the rules, and who checks that decider?
How do students who lost the election still get heard?
What happens when the council and the principal disagree?
How can the rules be changed later without one group rewriting them for itself?
stakeholders: Students who lose or never run
Clubs that depend on the budget
Next year's students who inherit the rules
criteria: Power is split among at least three roles or groups with different jobs
Every power has a check: name the counter-move for each
There is a way to change the rules that requires more than a simple majority
The proposal names one way it protects students who are not in the majority
Uses at least four glossary words correctly
constraints: Under two pages for the constitution itself, plus the half-page stress test
Nothing the principal cannot legally allow
Must work with 20 council members or with 8
Every rule must be explained with a reason, not just stated
brief.deliverable: A two-page proposed constitution with sections for powers, checks, the amendment rule, and protections for the minority, plus a half-page 'what if the wrong person wins?' test showing how the rules would hold.

factReview.note: AI-assisted content correction; no educator approval asserted.

parallelExample.context: A robotics club kept losing its budget to whichever member was loudest.
parallelExample.move: They split the roles: a treasurer who could spend, a two-member finance committee that had to approve any spending over $50, and an all-club vote that could reverse both. Spending got slower and the complaints stopped, because no single person could decide alone.
parallelExample.whyItHelps: It is the framers' move at club scale: separate the power to spend from the power to approve, and give the whole group a final check.

supports.frameStarter: If the wrong person became ____, they could ____. So we give the ____ the power to ____, and the ____ can answer by ____.
frameChoices: Separate who proposes spending from who approves it
Give a rules committee the power to strike down a decision that breaks the constitution
Require a two-thirds vote to change the rules
Guarantee any group of ten students the right to put an item on the agenda
coachPrompts: Which of your checks could a clever council president get around, and how would you close that gap?
Is your council too slow to plan a dance in time, and is that a bug or a feature?
Who protects a student who is not popular?

data.coachHint: Test every rule against a bad actor, not a good one. The framers assumed selfish operators and built for them.
data.sourceExcerpt: Their problem was not how to build a government. Their problem was how to build one that would still be safe when the wrong people were running it.
